KDIGO 2024　·　In review

Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic investigation?

A 60-year-old man presents to nephrology with fatigue and a new purpuric rash over the lower limbs. His past medical history includes hypertension. His current medications include amlodipine. Two weeks ago, blood tests showed a serum creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 77 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 84 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.0 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.2 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 21 mL/min/1.73 m2. Anti-proteinase 3 antibody and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody testing by antigen-specific immunoassays are negative. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.7 g/day. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic investigation?

A Complete blood count
B Repeat anti-proteinase 3 and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody testing
C C-reactive protein measurement
D Kidney biopsy
E Serum complement C3 and C4 measurement
Answer and explanation

D. Kidney biopsy

The key finding is the rapid numerical decline in kidney function together with an active glomerular urine sediment and moderate proteinuria. Serum creatinine has increased from 1.1 mg/dL to 3.2 mg/dL over two weeks, while the estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 77 to 21 mL/min/1.73 m2. These findings are compatible with necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis in the appropriate clinical setting. According to KDIGO, approximately 90% of patients with small-vessel vasculitis or necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis have ANCA directed mainly against myeloperoxidase or proteinase 3, but negative ANCA testing does not exclude the diagnosis. When the clinical presentation is compatible with a primary small-vessel vasculitis, both proteinase 3 ANCA and myeloperoxidase ANCA are negative, and there is no contraindication to biopsy, kidney biopsy is the appropriate next diagnostic investigation.

KDIGO 2024　·　In review

Which of the following serologic testing strategies is most appropriate at this time?

A 36-year-old man presents with a 9-day history of fatigue and cough. Over the past 4 days, he has developed increasing shortness of breath and several episodes of blood-streaked sputum. He has no known history of kidney disease. His current medications include no prescription medications. Twelve days ago, his serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 109 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 144/86 mmHg, heart rate is 102 beats per minute, temperature is 37.2 C, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.4 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. Chest imaging demonstrates bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.9 g/day. Which of the following serologic testing strategies is most appropriate at this time?

A Test for proteinase 3 ANCA and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies without myeloperoxidase ANCA testing
B Test for myeloperoxidase ANCA and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies without proteinase 3 ANCA testing
C Test for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA using antigen-specific immunoassays, together with anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies
D Test for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA without anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody testing
E Test for anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies without myeloperoxidase ANCA or proteinase 3 ANCA testing
Answer and explanation

C. Test for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA using antigen-specific immunoassays, together with anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies

The patient has concurrent pulmonary and glomerular kidney findings. He has blood-streaked sputum, hypoxemia, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates together with a rapid decline in kidney function. His serum creatinine has increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 3.4 mg/dL over 12 days, while his estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 109 to 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. Dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts further indicate glomerular kidney injury. According to KDIGO, simultaneous lung and kidney injury should raise concern for vasculitis, and serologic testing is of major diagnostic importance. A positive myeloperoxidase ANCA or proteinase 3 ANCA supports ANCA-associated vasculitis, whereas a positive anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody test suggests anti-glomerular basement membrane disease. High-quality antigen-specific immunoassays are the preferred screening method for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA.

KDIGO 2024　·　In review

Which of the following best describes the kidney lesion in this patient?

A 52-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nasal congestion, and reduced appetite. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine. Two weeks ago, serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 67 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 150/88 mmHg, heart rate is 92 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.3 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.1 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 17 mL/min/1.73 m2. Anti-proteinase 3 antibody testing is positive. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 2.1 g/day. A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 18 glomeruli, with segmental fibrinoid necrosis in 5 glomeruli and cellular crescents in 7 glomeruli. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits. Which of the following best describes the kidney lesion in this patient?

A Anti-glomerular basement membrane crescentic glomerulonephritis
B Pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis
C Immune-complex necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis
D Immunoglobulin A nephropathy with crescent formation
E C3-dominant glomerulonephritis with crescent formation
Answer and explanation

B. Pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis

The patient has rapidly progressive glomerular kidney injury. Serum creatinine has increased from 1.0 mg/dL to 3.1 mg/dL over two weeks, with a decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate from 67 to 17 mL/min/1.73 m2. The urine sediment demonstrates microscopic hematuria, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts, while proteinuria is moderate at 2.1 g/day. Positive proteinase 3 ANCA further supports an ANCA-associated vasculitic process in this clinical setting. The characteristic kidney lesion associated with ANCA-associated vasculitis is pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis. In this patient, light microscopy demonstrates focal segmental fibrinoid necrosis and cellular crescents, while immunofluorescence shows little or no immune deposition and electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense deposits. Together, these findings establish the pauci-immune pattern.

KDIGO 2024　·　In review

Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the negative anti-proteinase 3 and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody results?

A 57-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nasal congestion, and a new purpuric rash over the lower limbs. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine. Three weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 74 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 148/88 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.2 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.0 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 18 mL/min/1.73 m2. Anti-proteinase 3 antibody and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody testing by antigen-specific immunoassays are negative. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.8 g/day. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the negative anti-proteinase 3 and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody results?

A The negative antibody results establish an immune-complex glomerulonephritis as the most likely cause of the kidney findings
B ANCA-associated vasculitis is excluded because both major antigen-specific antibody tests are negative
C Pauci-immune necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis is excluded because ANCA must be detectable when kidney involvement is present
D The negative antibody results indicate that the decline in kidney function is unlikely to result from small-vessel vasculitis
E ANCA-associated vasculitis remains a possible diagnosis despite negative serologic testing
Answer and explanation

E. ANCA-associated vasculitis remains a possible diagnosis despite negative serologic testing

The patient has a clinical presentation compatible with small-vessel vasculitis involving the kidney. Her serum creatinine has increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 3.0 mg/dL over three weeks, while her estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 74 to 18 mL/min/1.73 m2. The urine sediment demonstrates glomerular hematuria with dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts, together with moderate proteinuria. According to KDIGO, approximately 90% of patients with small-vessel vasculitis or necrotizing and crescentic glomerulonephritis have ANCA, directed primarily against myeloperoxidase or proteinase 3. However, ANCA negativity does not exclude the diagnosis. The negative anti-proteinase 3 and anti-myeloperoxidase antibody results therefore reduce the serologic support for ANCA-associated vasculitis but do not eliminate it when the clinical presentation remains compatible.

KDIGO 2024　·　In review

Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the positive anti-proteinase 3 antibody result?

A 58-year-old woman is referred to nephrology after anti-proteinase 3 antibody testing obtained during an evaluation for several weeks of fatigue returns positive. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine. Her blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg, heart rate is 80 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.9 C. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 76 mL/min/1.73 m2, unchanged from measurements three months earlier. Complete blood count shows a hemoglobin level of 13.1 g/dL, white blood cell count of 6,800 cells per microliter, and platelet count of 248,000 cells per microliter. C-reactive protein is 3 mg/L. She reports no hemoptysis, shortness of breath, purpuric skin lesions, visual symptoms, or neurologic symptoms. Chest imaging shows no pulmonary infiltrates. Urinalysis demonstrates no blood, trace protein, 0 to 2 red blood cells per high-power field, and no red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 0.1 g/day. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of the positive anti-proteinase 3 antibody result?

A The result should be disregarded because ANCA testing has diagnostic value only when kidney dysfunction is already present
B The result establishes ANCA-associated vasculitis regardless of the absence of compatible clinical manifestations
C The result establishes granulomatosis with polyangiitis because proteinase 3 ANCA is positive
D The result establishes active kidney vasculitis despite the normal kidney function and urine sediment
E The result supports ANCA-associated vasculitis but must be interpreted together with the patient’s clinical findings, imaging, and other laboratory results
Answer and explanation

E. The result supports ANCA-associated vasculitis but must be interpreted together with the patient’s clinical findings, imaging, and other laboratory results

A positive proteinase 3 ANCA can support a diagnosis of ANCA-associated vasculitis, but it does not establish the diagnosis by itself. In this patient, kidney function is stable, the urine sediment does not show glomerular hematuria or red blood cell casts, quantified proteinuria is minimal, chest imaging is unremarkable, and there are no clear extrarenal manifestations of small-vessel vasculitis. According to KDIGO, the diagnosis of ANCA-associated vasculitis relies on the combination of clinical findings and the results of imaging studies and laboratory tests. Relevant laboratory assessment may include C-reactive protein, complete blood count, kidney parameters, urine sediment analysis, and antigen-specific testing for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA. A positive proteinase 3 ANCA result therefore provides diagnostic support only when interpreted within the overall clinical context.

KDIGO 2024　·　In review

Which of the following is the preferred initial ANCA screening strategy in this patient?

A 46-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nasal congestion, and a persistent cough. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine. Three weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 78 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.2 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 2.8 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. The combination of upper respiratory symptoms and rapidly declining kidney function raises concern for a small-vessel vasculitic process. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood, 2+ protein, 25 to 35 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.6 g/day. Which of the following is the preferred initial ANCA screening strategy in this patient?

A Anti-myeloperoxidase antibody testing alone because kidney involvement is present
B Indirect immunofluorescence for ANCA alone without antigen-specific testing
C Indirect immunofluorescence first, with myeloperoxidase and proteinase 3 antigen-specific testing only if the initial result is positive
D Anti-proteinase 3 antibody testing alone because upper respiratory manifestations are present
E High-quality antigen-specific immunoassays for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA
Answer and explanation

E. High-quality antigen-specific immunoassays for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA

The patient has findings that warrant evaluation for ANCA-associated vasculitis, including upper respiratory manifestations, a rapid numerical decline in kidney function, microscopic hematuria with dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts, and moderate proteinuria. Her serum creatinine has increased from 0.9 mg/dL to 2.8 mg/dL over three weeks, while her estimated glomerular filtration rate has fallen from 78 to 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. According to the revised international consensus cited by KDIGO, high-quality antigen-specific immunoassays are the preferred screening method for myeloperoxidase ANCA and proteinase 3 ANCA in patients being evaluated for granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis.

KDIGO 2024　·　In review

Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic approach at this time?

A 63-year-old woman presents with fatigue, reduced appetite, and aching in both knees and ankles. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine. Two weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 0.8 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 84 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 152/88 mmHg, heart rate is 94 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.3 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.0 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 17 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urine dipstick demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein. Urine microscopy shows 35 to 45 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, red blood cell casts, and 8 to 10 white blood cells per high-power field. Urine culture shows no bacterial growth. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.9 g/day. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic approach at this time?

A Obtain ANCA testing alone and proceed with further evaluation only if positive
B Evaluate primarily for a nonglomerular cause of acute kidney injury because the rise in serum creatinine is the dominant abnormality
C Repeat serum creatinine and urinalysis after several days before pursuing further diagnostic testing
D Evaluate for possible glomerular disease by obtaining autoimmune serologies, assess for systemic features, exclude infection, and consider kidney biopsy if appropriate
E Obtain kidney imaging to evaluate for urinary tract obstruction before any further workup
Answer and explanation

D. Evaluate for possible glomerular disease by obtaining autoimmune serologies, assess for systemic features, exclude infection, and consider kidney biopsy if appropriate

The patient has a rapid decline in kidney function over a short period, with serum creatinine rising from 0.8 mg/dL to 3.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate falling from 84 to 17 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria, and urine microscopy demonstrates dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts, which are characteristic of glomerular injury. The presence of pyuria with a negative urine culture further supports a noninfectious inflammatory renal process. This pattern is most consistent with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. The appropriate diagnostic approach is a broad evaluation for immune-mediated glomerular disease, including serologic testing (ANCA, anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, and complement levels), assessment for systemic manifestations, exclusion of infection, and kidney biopsy when feasible.

KDIGO 2024　·　In review

Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic direction at this time?

A 67-year-old man presents with fatigue, reduced appetite, and decreased urine output. His past medical history includes hypertension. His current medications include amlodipine. Six days ago, his serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 79 mL/min/1.73 m2. His blood pressure today is 138/82 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.9 C. Blood tests now show a serum creatinine of 3.1 mg/dL and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urine dipstick shows no blood and trace protein. Urine microscopy demonstrates 0 to 2 red blood cells per high-power field, no dysmorphic red blood cells, no red blood cell casts, and 1 to 2 white blood cells per high-power field. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 0.1 g/day. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic direction at this time?

A Evaluate specifically for ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis despite the absence of glomerular urine findings
B Evaluate for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with autoimmune serologies and kidney biopsy
C Evaluate for a nonglomerular cause of acute kidney injury
D Evaluate for anti-glomerular basement membrane disease as the primary explanation for the kidney dysfunction
E Evaluate for immune-complex glomerulonephritis based on the rapid decline in kidney function alone
Answer and explanation

C. Evaluate for a nonglomerular cause of acute kidney injury

The patient has developed a substantial decline in kidney function over six days, with serum creatinine increasing from 1.0 mg/dL to 3.1 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate falling from 79 to 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. However, the urine findings do not indicate a glomerular process. The dipstick shows no blood and only trace protein, while microscopy shows no glomerular hematuria, dysmorphic red blood cells, red blood cell casts, or pyuria. The diagnostic strategy in KDIGO distinguishes rapid kidney-function decline accompanied by glomerular urine abnormalities from rapid kidney-function decline without those abnormalities. When blood and protein are not present in the expected glomerular pattern, or when the urine sediment does not demonstrate glomerular hematuria or pyuria without infection, the appropriate direction is to evaluate for a nonglomerular cause of acute kidney injury.

KDIGO 2024　·　In review

According to the histopathologic classification of ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, which class best describes this biopsy?

A 52-year-old woman with newly diagnosed myeloperoxidase ANCA-associated vasculitis presents with fatigue, arthralgia, and declining kidney function. Her past medical history includes hypertension. Her current medications include amlodipine. Three weeks ago, her serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 68 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate is 88 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 2.9 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 19 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.8 g/day. A kidney biopsy is performed. Light microscopy shows 20 glomeruli. Three glomeruli are globally sclerotic, 10 are normal, and 7 contain cellular crescents, with focal segmental fibrinoid necrosis also present. Immunofluorescence shows no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy shows no significant electron-dense immune deposits. According to the histopathologic classification of ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, which class best describes this biopsy?

A Not classifiable within the histopathologic system
B Crescentic class
C Sclerotic class
D Mixed class
E Focal class
Answer and explanation

E. Focal class

The biopsy contains 20 glomeruli. Three of 20 glomeruli, or 15%, are globally sclerotic; 10 of 20, or 50%, are normal; and 7 of 20, or 35%, contain cellular crescents. The histopathologic classification should be applied in a specific sequence. A biopsy is classified as sclerotic when at least 50% of glomeruli are globally sclerotic. If this criterion is not met, the next step is to determine whether at least 50% of glomeruli are normal. If so, the biopsy is classified as focal. Only if neither of these criteria is satisfied is the proportion of glomeruli with cellular crescents considered; at least 50% cellular crescents defines the crescentic class. Biopsies that meet none of these predominant patterns are classified as mixed.

KDIGO 2024　·　In review

When counseling the patient about long-term kidney outcomes, which of the following biopsy profiles would be associated with the most favorable prognosis based on validation studies of the Berden histopathologic classification?

A 64-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of fatigue, reduced appetite, and a purpuric rash over both lower limbs. She has no known history of chronic kidney disease. Her current medications include amlodipine for hypertension. One month ago, her serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate was 63 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her blood pressure today is 150/88 mmHg, heart rate is 90 beats per minute, and temperature is 37.1 C. Serum creatinine is now 3.2 mg/dL and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 16 mL/min/1.73 m2. Myeloperoxidase ANCA testing is positive. Urinalysis demonstrates 3+ blood and 2+ protein, with 30 to 40 red blood cells per high-power field, dysmorphic red blood cells, and red blood cell casts. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.9 g/day. The clinical findings are consistent with newly diagnosed ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis, and a kidney biopsy is planned to provide additional prognostic information. When counseling the patient about long-term kidney outcomes, which of the following biopsy profiles would be associated with the most favorable prognosis based on validation studies of the Berden histopathologic classification?

A 20% normal glomeruli, 60% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 20% glomeruli with cellular crescents
B 60% normal glomeruli, 20% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 20% glomeruli with cellular crescents
C 30% normal glomeruli, 25% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 45% glomeruli with cellular crescents
D 45% normal glomeruli, 30% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 25% glomeruli with cellular crescents
E 25% normal glomeruli, 40% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 35% glomeruli with cellular crescents
Answer and explanation

B. 60% normal glomeruli, 20% globally sclerotic glomeruli, and 20% glomeruli with cellular crescents

Kidney histology provides prognostic information in ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis. In validation studies of the Berden histopathologic classification, more than 50% normal glomeruli in the focal class were associated with a favorable kidney outcome, whereas more than 50% globally sclerotic glomeruli were associated with a poor outcome. Outcomes reported for the crescentic and mixed classes have been less consistent.

KDIGO 2024　·　In review

Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

A 56-year-old man with proteinase 3 ANCA-associated vasculitis was diagnosed three months ago after presenting with fatigue, nasal congestion, purpura, and rapidly declining kidney function. At diagnosis, his serum creatinine was 3.1 mg/dL, and his estimated glomerular filtration rate was 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. A kidney biopsy was performed, and induction therapy was started. Six weeks after starting treatment, his extrarenal symptoms had improved, C-reactive protein had decreased from 48 mg/L to 4 mg/L, and kidney function had partially improved. His serum creatinine decreased to 2.5 mg/dL, and his estimated glomerular filtration rate increased to 30 mL/min/1.73 m2. Over the next six weeks, despite continued treatment, his kidney function worsened. At the current visit, serum creatinine has increased to 3.2 mg/dL, and estimated glomerular filtration rate has decreased to 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. His nasal symptoms, purpura, and constitutional symptoms remain resolved. His blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg, heart rate is 80 beats per minute, and temperature is 36.9 C. Urinalysis demonstrates 2+ blood and 2+ protein, with 15 to 20 red blood cells per high-power field. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio estimates proteinuria of 1.3 g/day. The treating team is uncertain whether the worsening kidney function reflects ongoing vasculitic activity, residual parenchymal damage, or another kidney process. The initial kidney biopsy showed focal segmental fibrinoid necrosis and cellular crescents on light microscopy, with areas of interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy. Immunofluorescence showed no significant glomerular staining for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, or C1q. Electron microscopy showed no significant electron-dense immune deposits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

A Repeat proteinase 3 ANCA testing to determine whether renal vasculitis remains active
B Repeat kidney biopsy to reassess renal histologic activity and chronic damage
C Repeat C-reactive protein measurement to determine whether kidney inflammation persists
D Obtain renal ultrasonography to determine whether the kidney dysfunction reflects active vasculitis
E Repeat urine protein quantification to determine whether the current kidney injury is reversible
Answer and explanation

B. Repeat kidney biopsy to reassess renal histologic activity and chronic damage

The patient initially improved after treatment. His extrarenal manifestations resolved, C-reactive protein normalized, and kidney function partially recovered, with serum creatinine decreasing from 3.1 mg/dL to 2.5 mg/dL. However, during the following six weeks, kidney function worsened despite continued treatment. Serum creatinine increased to 3.2 mg/dL, and estimated glomerular filtration rate decreased to 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. Hematuria and proteinuria also persist. According to KDIGO, assessing kidney remission can be difficult because hematuria and proteinuria may persist after treatment. Stable or falling serum creatinine, control of extrarenal disease, and normalization of inflammatory markers are helpful, but they do not exclude ongoing kidney activity. Other causes of kidney injury unrelated to ANCA-associated vasculitis should also be considered. When treatment response is poor or the cause of persistent kidney dysfunction remains uncertain, repeat kidney biopsy should be considered.
